A Frobenius group G = K ⋊ H where K is the Frobenius kernel (normal) and H is the complement (point stabilizer). The kernel is an elementary abelian p-group, so K ≅ (C_p)^n for some n. The complement H acts on K \ {1} fixed-point-freely (each non-identity element of H fixes only identity in K).

2-transitive: G acts 2-transitively on the cosets of H (or equivalently on K since K is regular). A Frobenius group is 2-transitive iff the complement H acts transitively on K \ {1}.

So H acts transitively on K \ {1}. Since K is elementary abelian of order p^n, |K \ {1}| = p^n - 1. H acts transitively on these p^n - 1 elements.

The question: is H always abelian?

This is related to the classification of 2-transitive groups with elementary abelian regular normal subgroup. These are exactly the affine 2-transitive groups.

By Hering's classification (or the classification of 2-transitive permutation groups), the affine 2-transitive groups where the point stabilizer acts transitively on non-zero vectors are classified. The complement H ≤ GL(n, p) acts transitively on nonzero vectors.

The question is whether H must be abelian.

Counterexample: Consider AGL(1, q) where q = p^n. This is the group of affine transformations x → ax + b with a ∈ F_q^*, b ∈ F_q. The kernel is (F_q, +) ≅ (C_p)^n, the complement is F_q^* which is cyclic, hence abelian. So this gives abelian complement.

But there are non-abelian examples. Consider AGL(n, p) for n ≥ 2 with the full GL(n,p) as complement. GL(n,p) acts transitively on nonzero vectors? No, GL(n,p) acts transitively on nonzero vectors (yes it does! Any nonzero vector can be sent to any other nonzero vector by a linear map). So AGL(n,p) is 2-transitive, kernel is elementary abelian, complement GL(n,p) is non-abelian for n ≥ 2 (and n=1 gives abelian).

Wait, but is AGL(n,p) a Frobenius group? A Frobenius group requires that the complement acts fixed-point-freely: every non-identity element of H fixes only the identity in K.

In AGL(n,p), the complement is GL(n,p). Does every non-identity element of GL(n,p) act fixed-point-freely on K = (F_p)^n? No! For example, a reflection or any element with eigenvalue 1 fixes nonzero vectors. So GL(n,p) does NOT act fixed-point-freely. So AGL(n,p) is 2-transitive but NOT a Frobenius group (for n ≥ 2).
